issues.legal_issue: A conviction entered after reversal of an acquittal is unsustainable when the trial court’s view remains at least as acceptable as the appellate court’s view on the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused only for injuring one person and acquitted him of the charge relating to the death of another person.
The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted the accused of murder with common intention.

The first information report, made several hours after the occurrence by the deceased’s father, did not say that the accused had stabbed the deceased; the alleged eyewitnesses and the alleged dying declaration were also not mentioned as such in it.

The evidence about where the stabbing took place was uncertain, the site plans did not record where blood was found, and the medical evidence cast doubt on the account that the deceased had moved after being stabbed or made the alleged declaration.

The Court found the alleged eyewitness accounts not credible and the alleged dying declaration unreliable, and considered the trial court’s view that the deceased had been stabbed by another accused in the lane more likely.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s view was at least as acceptable as the High Court’s view, so the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s murder conviction and sentence.
issues.legal_principle: On an appeal against acquittal, an appellate court should not interfere merely because it can adopt one of two reasonably possible views favouring conviction; it may interfere if the trial court’s view is not reasonably sustainable on the evidence. When the High Court reverses an acquittal and convicts, the Supreme Court may set aside that decision if, after considering the cases and crucial evidence, the trial court’s view is at least as acceptable as the High Court’s. No earlier case is cited for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_acquittal_reversal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which an appellate court reversed a trial court’s acquittal and convicted the accused.
predicates.trial_view_at_least_as_acceptable: The evidence leaves the trial court’s view at least as acceptable as the view supporting the appellate conviction.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a conviction entered after reversal of an acquittal, the conviction is set aside if the trial court’s view remains at least as acceptable on the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: An omission of an important fact from a first information report may be relevant to assessing the veracity of the prosecution case under the rule concerning facts affecting probabilities.
material_facts: The deceased’s father made the first information report about four hours after the incident.
The report described the occurrence but did not state that the accused had stabbed the deceased.

The Court considered that important facts of the occurrence would have been communicated to the father by the time he made the report, and that the omission bore on the probabilities of the prosecution account.
issues.conclusion: The omission of the accused’s alleged participation was relevant under Section 11 of the Evidence Act in judging the veracity of the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: A first information report is a previous statement that, strictly speaking, may be used to corroborate or contradict its maker. Under Section 11 of the Evidence Act, an omission of an important fact may also be relevant to assess the probabilities and veracity of the prosecution case in the circumstances. No earlier case is cited for this principle.

predicates.criminal_case_evidence_assessment: The evidence is being assessed in a criminal case.
predicates.informed_report_maker_omitted_material_p: A person who had been informed of the important circumstances made a report but omitted the accused’s alleged participation in the central event.

issues.definition: In assessing evidence in a criminal case, an informed report maker’s omission of alleged participation in the central event is relevant to the prosecution’s veracity.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction based on common intention is not justified where the appellate court finds that the accused were individually responsible for their acts and that there was no preconcert to commit an offence.
material_facts: The High Court found that the accused did not arrive together, that there was nothing to show a preconcert to commit an offence, and that the incident took an unexpected turn.
The High Court also found that the accused and another person were individually responsible for their acts, but nevertheless convicted the accused of murder with common intention.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in convicting the accused of murder with common intention on the findings it had made.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, which provides for joint responsibility for an act done in furtherance of a common intention. On the High Court’s findings of individual responsibility and no preconcert, the conviction under Sections 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code could not stand. No earlier case is cited for this application.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_common_inten: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction based on shared responsibility for an offence.
predicates.individual_responsibility_found: The court found that the accused were individually responsible for their respective acts.
predicates.preconcert_absent: The court found no evidence that the accused had concerted beforehand to commit an offence.

issues.definition: A conviction based on shared responsibility is unsustainable in a criminal appeal when the court found individual responsibility and no preconcert.

issues.legal_issue: An accused may appeal to the Supreme Court as of right when an acquittal has been converted into a conviction carrying a life sentence, without obtaining a certificate from the High Court.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused of the charge concerning the death.
The High Court reversed that acquittal, convicted the accused of murder with common intention, and imposed a life sentence.
The appeal came to the Supreme Court with a High Court certificate, but the Court held that such a certificate was unnecessary.
issues.conclusion: The accused’s appeal lay to the Supreme Court as a matter of right, and no High Court certificate was required.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, an appeal lies as of right when an acquittal is converted into a conviction and a life sentence is imposed; a High Court certificate is not necessary.

predicates.criminal_appeal_to_supreme_court: The proceeding is an accused’s criminal appeal to the Supreme Court.
predicates.acquittal_converted_to_conviction: An appellate court converted the accused’s acquittal into a conviction.
predicates.life_sentence_imposed: The appellate court imposed a life sentence on the accused.

issues.definition: An accused’s appeal to the Supreme Court lies as of right without a certificate when an appellate court has converted an acquittal into a conviction and imposed a life sentence.
